recommendations.title: Follow their topic
recommendations.what_to_do: During a familiar routine, notice what catches your child’s interest. Make one short comment and leave space for any response.
recommendations.why_this: Following what already has their attention is the easiest way in to a two-way exchange.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether and how they respond

recommendations.title: Copy a small movement
recommendations.what_to_do: Invite your child to choose a comfortable movement for you to copy. Swap roles only if they want to.
recommendations.why_this: Copying a movement they chose keeps it at a level they can manage.
recommendations.you_might_notice: The movement chosen and help wanted

recommendations.title: Name and stay nearby
recommendations.what_to_do: After a small frustration, offer a tentative feeling word and stay available. Accept a correction or silence.
recommendations.why_this: Naming what you see and staying close is support they can use before they have the words.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What happened and what support was welcomed

recommendations.title: Choose one routine step
recommendations.what_to_do: Offer one safe part of an everyday routine for your child to try, with help nearby. Let them ask you to finish.
recommendations.why_this: One real choice inside a routine is independence at a size they can carry.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which part they attempted and the assistance given

recommendations.title: Make space to join
recommendations.what_to_do: Sit near an existing play activity. Offer your participation without requiring sharing or conversation.
recommendations.why_this: Leaving space to join, rather than asking, lets them choose company on their own terms.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether your invitation was accepted

recommendations.title: A page chosen together
recommendations.what_to_do: Let your child choose a familiar page. Talk about one detail they notice; finishing the book is optional.
recommendations.why_this: A page they chose is a page they will talk about.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Their chosen detail and response

recommendations.title: Find a pair
recommendations.skill: How many, and which is more
recommendations.what_to_do: Put out a few large safe objects. Invite your child to find two that belong together in a way they choose.
recommendations.why_this: Matching a pair is the first sorting rule, using things already in the room.
recommendations.you_might_notice: The grouping they made, with no right-answer score

recommendations.title: Notice a change
recommendations.what_to_do: Look together at something familiar, such as the view from a window. Invite a comment about what is different today.
recommendations.why_this: Noticing a change is the beginning of comparing and asking why.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What your child points to or describes

recommendations.title: Invent a pretend sound
recommendations.what_to_do: Follow a pretend-play idea your child starts. Offer a sound for your role and let them change the story.
recommendations.why_this: A pretend sound they invented is theirs to keep or change.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Their idea and how the play continued

recommendations.title: Add one word back
recommendations.what_to_do: When your child says a word or a short phrase, say it back with one word added. “Dog.” → “Big dog.” Then wait. Do this a few times during an ordinary routine such as getting dressed or a meal.
recommendations.why_this: A slightly longer version of their own words gives them the next step without a correction.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they look, repeat, add anything or move on

recommendations.title: Name what they are holding
recommendations.what_to_do: Sit beside your child while they play. Name the thing they are holding or looking at, once, in a short phrase. Leave a pause before saying anything else.
recommendations.why_this: Words land best when they arrive at the moment the child is already looking.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What holds their attention and whether they respond to the naming

recommendations.title: A two-object retelling
recommendations.what_to_do: Take two familiar objects and act out something that happened today in two or three moves — the cup went on the table, the cup fell over. Let your child hold or move one object if they want.
recommendations.why_this: Acting out a tiny event gives order to talk about before the words for order arrive.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they join in, copy a move or add their own

recommendations.title: What happened next?
recommendations.what_to_do: After a small everyday event — a spill, a visitor, a bird outside — say what you saw in one sentence and ask “and then?”. Accept any answer, including none. Add one detail of your own if they stop.
recommendations.why_this: Retelling in order is practice at holding a sequence in mind, with you filling gaps.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they order events and which details they choose

recommendations.title: Answer their question with a question back
recommendations.what_to_do: When your child asks a “why” or “what” question, answer briefly, then ask one open question of your own — “What do you think it does?”. Follow whatever they say next rather than correcting it.
recommendations.why_this: A question handed back keeps the exchange going and lets them do more of the talking.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they extend the topic and for how long

recommendations.title: A pretend phone call
recommendations.what_to_do: Hold a block or hand to your ear and “ring” your child about something ordinary — what is for lunch, where their shoes are. Let them decide when the call ends.
recommendations.why_this: Pretend calls invite turn-taking talk with no right answers to get wrong.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How many turns they take and who they choose to be

recommendations.title: Carry it to the box
recommendations.what_to_do: Ask your child to carry one light, familiar thing — a soft toy, a sock — a few steps to a box or basket. Walk with them. Repeat only while they want to.
recommendations.why_this: Carrying something light over a short distance is everyday practice at balance and grip.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they hold the object and whether they choose to keep going

recommendations.title: Slow walk, fast walk
recommendations.what_to_do: Walk across the room together, first slowly, then a little faster, then slowly again. Say the word as you do it. No running indoors; keep to a clear space.
recommendations.why_this: Changing pace on purpose is control practice inside an ordinary walk.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they change pace with you and which they prefer

recommendations.title: Reach up, reach down
recommendations.what_to_do: Hold a soft toy a little above their reach and then near the floor. Invite them to take it and put it somewhere you point to. Stay within easy reach and keep both feet on the floor.
recommendations.why_this: Reaching high and low with both feet planted asks for steadiness without any risk.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they reach, bend and steady themselves

recommendations.title: Animal walks
recommendations.what_to_do: Take turns choosing an animal and moving like it across the room — a slow tortoise, a hopping frog, a tall giraffe. Stay on a clear, non-slip floor and keep it to a few turns.
recommendations.why_this: Varied movement across the day matters more than any one exercise; this adds variety in minutes.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which movements they choose and how they manage balance and stopping

recommendations.title: Roll and stop
recommendations.what_to_do: Sit facing each other on the floor a short distance apart and roll a soft ball to each other. Add a rule together — stop it with a hand, then a foot. Keep the ball soft and the space clear.
recommendations.why_this: Tracking a rolling ball and stopping it is eye–hand–foot practice with a rule they helped make.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they track the ball and whether they hold the rule you agreed

recommendations.title: Outside at their pace
recommendations.what_to_do: On any short outdoor walk, let your child set the pace and choose one thing to stop and look at. Do not hurry the stop; end when they are ready or when your time is up.
recommendations.why_this: Time outside at their own pace counts towards a whole day of movement, without a plan.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What they stop for and how long they stay with it

recommendations.title: Name the moment, then wait
recommendations.what_to_do: When your child is clearly pleased, cross or sad, say what you see in a few words — “You wanted the red one.” — and stay close. Do not ask them to calm down or to answer.
recommendations.why_this: A calm adult putting the moment into words is what helps a big feeling pass.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What happens after the naming: settling, protest, moving on

recommendations.title: Teddy feels
recommendations.what_to_do: During play, give a soft toy an ordinary feeling — Teddy is tired, Teddy is happy the cup is back. Ask nothing; let your child respond to the toy however they like.
recommendations.why_this: A toy with a feeling lets them look at feelings from a safe distance.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they respond to the toy’s feeling and how

recommendations.title: A settling place
recommendations.what_to_do: Choose with your child one comfortable spot — a cushion, a lap, a corner — that they can go to when things feel too much. Show it once at a calm time. Never send them there; go together if they want.
recommendations.why_this: A place chosen in a calm moment is easier to reach for in a hard one.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they use it, and what helps them settle

recommendations.title: When the character is upset
recommendations.what_to_do: While reading or telling a story, pause when a character has an ordinary problem and wonder aloud — “I think she might feel cross. What do you think?”. Accept their answer, including “don’t know”.
recommendations.why_this: A character’s ordinary problem gives feelings a name without putting the child on the spot.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which feelings they name and whether they link them to what happened

recommendations.title: Body clues
recommendations.what_to_do: At a calm time, talk about what your own body does when you are excited or tired — fast feet, big yawn. Invite your child to show one. Keep it playful; no answers are wrong.
recommendations.why_this: Noticing what the body does is a first step towards knowing what a feeling is.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which clues they notice in themselves or in you

recommendations.title: After the storm
recommendations.what_to_do: Once an upset has fully passed, at a quiet moment, say one sentence about what happened and one about what helped — “The tower fell. Sitting with me helped.” Leave it there unless they add more.
recommendations.why_this: Looking back once things are calm shows that upsets end and that help was there.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they add to the account or want to leave it

recommendations.title: This or that
recommendations.what_to_do: At a routine moment, hold up two acceptable options — the blue cup or the green cup, socks first or shoes first — and let your child choose. Go with the choice.
recommendations.why_this: Two acceptable options give a real decision without an argument about the outcome.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they choose and whether they change their mind

recommendations.title: The last step is theirs
recommendations.what_to_do: In a routine you normally do for them, leave the final step for them — pulling the sock over the heel, pushing the drawer shut. Wait; help only if they ask or seem stuck.
recommendations.why_this: Finishing the last step themselves is the part of the routine they can own first.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which step they manage and whether they ask for help

recommendations.title: Put it back where it lives
recommendations.what_to_do: After play, choose one item together and ask where it lives. Let them carry it there. One item is enough; stop before it becomes tidying-up.
recommendations.why_this: Remembering where one thing lives is a small, complete job.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they remember the place and want to do another

recommendations.title: A two-step job
recommendations.what_to_do: Ask your child to do a small job with two parts — get the spoon, then put it on the table. Say both parts once, then wait. If they do one, say the second again without correcting.
recommendations.why_this: Holding two steps in mind is practice at planning, in a job that matters to the family.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they hold both steps and what they do if they forget

recommendations.title: You choose the order
recommendations.what_to_do: Before a familiar routine such as getting ready, ask which of two things they will do first. Follow their order. If it does not work well, note it together without blame.
recommendations.why_this: Choosing the order and seeing how it goes is planning with a safe result either way.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they decide and whether they stick to the plan

recommendations.title: Make part of a snack
recommendations.what_to_do: Let your child do one safe part of preparing a snack — spreading with a blunt knife, tearing lettuce, putting fruit in a bowl. Stay beside them; you handle anything sharp or hot.
recommendations.why_this: A real part of a real snack is hand control and independence at once.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What they can manage with their hands and how they respond to a wobble

recommendations.title: Pass it back
recommendations.what_to_do: Sit with your child and pass a toy back and forth. Say “your turn” and “my turn”. If they keep it, let them; try again another time.
recommendations.why_this: Passing a toy is the simplest possible turn, with the waiting kept short.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they wait for a turn and how long the game lasts

recommendations.title: Help me carry
recommendations.what_to_do: Carry something ordinary together — one handle each of a small basket, or each holding an end of a towel. Walk it to where it goes and say “we did it”.
recommendations.why_this: A job that needs two people is a shared plan with a visible result.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they hold on and adjust to your pace

recommendations.title: Hello and goodbye
recommendations.what_to_do: At natural moments — a family member arriving, a neighbour passing — model a wave or a “hello” without asking your child to copy. Notice what they do on their own over the week.
recommendations.why_this: Seeing a greeting modelled, without being asked to copy, lets them try it when they are ready.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they wave, say hello, hide or watch

recommendations.title: Build one thing together
recommendations.what_to_do: Choose something to make together — a block tower, a den from cushions — where each of you adds a piece in turn. Let them decide when it is finished.
recommendations.why_this: Adding a piece in turn is a joint plan where each turn changes the outcome.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they take turns and respond when a piece goes somewhere unexpected

recommendations.title: Ask to join
recommendations.what_to_do: When your child is playing, ask “Can I play too?” and wait for an answer. If they say no, accept it and stay nearby. If yes, follow their rules for the game.
recommendations.why_this: Asking to join, and accepting a no, models how invitations work both ways.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they let you in, and what role they give you

recommendations.title: Share out the snack
recommendations.what_to_do: Give your child a small bowl of pieces to share between two or three people at the table, including themselves. Let them decide how; say nothing about fairness unless they ask.
recommendations.why_this: Dividing a snack is a real sharing decision with nothing at stake but the fun of it.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they divide it and whether they change it

recommendations.title: Point and name
recommendations.what_to_do: Open a picture book at any page. Let your child point to whatever they like; you name it in a short phrase. Follow their pointing; turn the page when they do.
recommendations.why_this: Naming what they point to ties words to pictures at their pace.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What they point to and whether they return to favourites

recommendations.title: The same book again
recommendations.what_to_do: Read the book your child chooses, even if it is the same one as yesterday. Pause before a familiar word or picture and see if they fill it in.
recommendations.why_this: A familiar book lets them predict and fill in, which is the start of reading along.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they anticipate a word, picture or page

recommendations.title: Big marks
recommendations.what_to_do: Put out a large piece of paper and one chunky crayon. Make a mark and describe it — “a long line”. Let your child make theirs. Describe, do not correct.
recommendations.why_this: Big marks with a chunky crayon build the hand control that later writing needs.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they hold the crayon and which marks they repeat

recommendations.title: What will happen?
recommendations.what_to_do: Before turning a page in a familiar story, ask what happens next. Any answer is fine; then read and see. Do this once or twice, not on every page.
recommendations.why_this: Predicting what comes next shows how much of the story they are holding.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they predict from memory or from the pictures

recommendations.title: Write the list for me
recommendations.what_to_do: Ask your child to “write” a shopping or packing list while you say the items. Their marks, scribbles or letter-like shapes are the list; take it with you and “read” it later.
recommendations.why_this: A list that gets used shows that marks on paper carry meaning.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which marks they make and whether they read them back

recommendations.title: Your name on your picture
recommendations.what_to_do: When your child finishes a drawing, offer to write their name on it, or let them make their own marks for their name. Say the letters as you write; do not ask them to copy.
recommendations.why_this: Their own name is the first word most children want to recognise.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they show interest in the letters or in making their own

recommendations.title: More or less
recommendations.skill: How many, and which is more
recommendations.what_to_do: At snack time put two small piles of the same food on the table, one clearly bigger. Ask which has more. Let them take the one they choose.
recommendations.why_this: Comparing two piles by eye is the start of thinking about amount.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they compare by looking and how they show it

recommendations.title: Sort the socks
recommendations.what_to_do: Tip out a few pairs of socks and sort them together — big and small, or by colour. Say what you are doing in short phrases. Stop when the interest goes.
recommendations.why_this: Sorting by one feature is a rule they can see and keep.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which feature they sort by and whether they keep the rule

recommendations.title: Count the steps
recommendations.what_to_do: While climbing a few stairs or taking a few steps, count them out loud together. Keep to the number of steps you actually take; there is no target.
recommendations.why_this: Counting real steps keeps the number words tied to real things.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they join in with the counting words and in what order

recommendations.title: Set the table for us
recommendations.what_to_do: Ask your child to put out one cup for each person at the table. If there is a spare or a gap, wonder about it together rather than correcting.
recommendations.why_this: One cup for each person is one-to-one matching with a purpose.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they match cups to people and what they do about a mismatch

recommendations.title: Make a pattern line
recommendations.what_to_do: Lay out a repeating line with two kinds of object — spoon, fork, spoon, fork. Ask what comes next. Then let your child start a line for you to continue.
recommendations.why_this: Continuing a pattern, then inventing one, is early maths inside play.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they continue the pattern and whether they invent their own

recommendations.title: Where is it?
recommendations.what_to_do: Hide a toy somewhere easy and describe where — under the cushion, behind the chair, next to the door. Then swap: they hide, you ask “where?” and they tell you.
recommendations.why_this: Position words are easier to learn while hiding and finding something.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which position words they use and understand

recommendations.title: Wet and dry
recommendations.what_to_do: At the sink or bath, touch a dry cloth and a wet one together. Say the words. Let your child squeeze, drip and compare. Keep water shallow and stay within reach.
recommendations.why_this: Comparing two states they can feel puts words to a difference they already notice.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What they do with the cloths and whether they use the words

recommendations.title: Look out of the window
recommendations.what_to_do: Stand at a window together for a minute or two. Name one thing that is moving and one that is still. Let your child point to whatever they notice.
recommendations.why_this: A minute at the window is looking closely, which is what science starts with.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What catches their attention and whether they point or name

recommendations.title: Push and pull
recommendations.what_to_do: With a toy car or a box on the floor, show a push and a pull. Say the words. Let them try both and see what moves further.
recommendations.why_this: Trying both and seeing what moves further is a small experiment.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they try both and which they repeat

recommendations.title: What changed since yesterday?
recommendations.what_to_do: Pick one thing in the home or garden — a plant, the sky, a puddle, a piece of fruit — and look at it two days running. Ask what is different. Accept any observation.
recommendations.why_this: Looking at the same thing twice is how noticing change begins.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What they notice and whether they remember the earlier look

recommendations.title: Sink or float
recommendations.what_to_do: At bath or sink time, choose a few safe objects and guess together whether each will sink or float before trying. Guessing wrong is part of it; no explanation needed.
recommendations.why_this: Guessing before testing is the habit of thinking ahead, and surprises are the fun part.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they guess, how they react to a surprise and whether they want to test more

recommendations.title: Ask the expert
recommendations.what_to_do: When your child seems to know something about an animal, vehicle or place, ask them to tell you about it as the expert. Listen; add one fact if they ask.
recommendations.why_this: Being asked to explain something they know shows what they have picked up and how they say it.
recommendations.you_might_notice: What they know already and how they explain it

recommendations.title: Two sounds
recommendations.what_to_do: Make a sound with something safe — tapping a pan lid with a wooden spoon, patting a cushion. Invite your child to make a different one. Take a few turns. Keep it quiet if noise is unwelcome.
recommendations.why_this: Making a different sound each turn is inventing, with nothing to get wrong.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which sounds they choose and whether they copy or invent

recommendations.title: Feed the toy
recommendations.what_to_do: Bring a cup or spoon to a soft toy and pretend to feed it. Offer the cup to your child without asking them to copy. Follow whatever they do with it.
recommendations.why_this: A cup offered to a toy is an open invitation to pretend, taken up or not.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Whether they join the pretend, change it or do something else

recommendations.title: Dance and stop
recommendations.what_to_do: Put on a short piece of music or sing. Move together, then stop when the music stops. Let your child choose how to move. Two or three rounds is plenty.
recommendations.why_this: Moving to music and stopping with it is rhythm and control in one game.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they move and whether they notice the stop

recommendations.title: What is this now?
recommendations.what_to_do: Hold up an ordinary object — a wooden spoon, a box — and pretend it is something else. Pass it over and ask “what is it now?”. Take turns; any idea counts.
recommendations.why_this: Turning one object into many is flexible thinking made visible.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How many ideas they offer and whether they build on yours

recommendations.title: A story from three things
recommendations.what_to_do: Put three familiar objects in front of you both and make up a very short story that uses all three. Let your child pick the objects, or the ending, or both.
recommendations.why_this: A story from three things is planning a small idea and seeing it through.
recommendations.you_might_notice: Which parts they contribute and whether they keep the plan or change it

recommendations.title: Draw the sound
recommendations.what_to_do: Make a sound — a hum, a tap, a whoosh — and draw a line for it on paper. Ask your child to draw one for a sound of their own. There is no right line.
recommendations.why_this: Drawing a sound joins two kinds of making with no right answer.
recommendations.you_might_notice: How they connect a sound to a mark and what they say about it
